China product export resumes

1⃣As discussed in the previous brief "The widely anticipated return of China from Golden Week", Reuters reported today that China has resumed October fuel exports at around 3.7 mt.

2⃣This number is about 700 kt lower than the September export allowance of 4.4 mt. However on a pro-rated basis (i.e. only 23 days to be exported out of 31 days), the reduction in export volume is fairly close. This indicates the pace of exports for the remaining part of the month should be similar to September.

3⃣The anticipated product impact remains unchanged from the first brief, where prompt regrade should weaken, prompt diesel spreads weaken.

4⃣Product cracks probably will suffer a knee-jerk reaction by weakening, but ultimately is bounded by refining margins needing to be positive. With dirty freight likely to remain stubbornly elevated and AG crude FOBs already adjusting weaker, my view is product cracks will be next to move up to keep the medium refining margins positive.

5⃣There was another report that the 3rd batch of product export quotas were released, 4.5 mt for CPP, 1.1 mt for LSFO.  Not surprisingly, the total export quota for 2026 is lower than 2025. This is not to be confused with the monthly quota that was introduced since mid this year as a tighter control from the Chinese government in view of the US-Iran war.

#Commodities: 

#Gold trades near USD 4,200, recovering from a challenging week that saw prices fall to a two-month low as bond yields surged to fresh multi-year highs. The rebound has been supported by a recovery in US Treasuries following a well-received 30-year bond auction, alongside some easing in oil prices, although fuel costs remain elevated. Gold ETF demand has remained remarkably resilient throughout the recent surge in yields, with total holdings rising to a fresh four-year high on Thursday. Combined with renewed Chinese demand following the Golden Week holiday, this underlying investment appetite is helping bullion recover and challenging recent attempts by short sellers to push prices lower.

Brent #crudeoil trades near USD 103, retreating from Thursday's high near USD 106 after Trump ruled out an attack on Iran ahead of the US midterm elections. This signals a potential three-week period of relative calm, which, provided Iran refrains from further escalation, could allow crude exports from the Gulf to remain elevated. However, the underlying stress in the oil market remains concentrated in refining capacity and the availability of refined products, particularly middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel. Gulf product exports are estimated at around 50% of pre-war levels (Kpler), highlighting the continued supply shortfall. A sustained recovery in refinery operations and product exports will therefore be essential before the market can begin to normalise, even as crude flows continue to improve.

The Bloomberg Commodity Total Return Index is heading for its first weekly gain in three, up 1.6% at the start of Friday’s session, lifting its year-to-date advance to 35%. Despite persistent macroeconomic headwinds, all sectors are contributing to the recovery, once again led by energy, where natural gas and particularly diesel futures have posted strong gains. Perhaps surprisingly, given how the week has unfolded, precious metals occupy second place, with gold heading for its best weekly performance since early August. Industrial metals are also trading higher, albeit with more modest gains led by copper and zinc. Agriculture is contributing with most grain and soft commodity futures posting small weekly gains, led by soybeans, corn, sugar and cotton.

Container freight costs: Global container freight rates have started to ease, with continued weakness on the Shanghai-to-Europe routes now being joined by the Shanghai-to-US lanes, following weeks of exceptional strength that drove shipping costs to Los Angeles and New York to four-year highs.

The Drewry Composite Index fell 2% this week to USD 4,351 per 40-foot container, but remains up 164% over the past year, with much of that increase (129%) occurring since the start of the Middle East conflict which triggered widespread disruptions to global shipping routes and supply chains.

The latest decline may partly reflect the seasonal winding down of peak shipping demand ahead of the Christmas shopping season, compounded by reduced Chinese factory activity during the Golden Week holiday. Meanwhile, increased vessel transits through the Suez Canal are helping ease capacity constraints on European routes.

However, underlying shipping costs remain elevated, not least because of continued restrictions at the Panama Canal, where El Niño-related water shortages have reduced transit capacity while rerouted energy shipments have increased competition for available slots. This has driven auction premiums sharply higher, adding to the cost of serving US East Coast destinations.

The recent easing therefore reflects some relief from seasonal demand and capacity pressures rather than a broader normalisation of global shipping conditions. With geopolitical disruptions continuing and key maritime chokepoints operating under constraints, freight rates remain vulnerable to renewed volatility.
